c.tagline: Gateway to Khiva – Silk Road Khorezm on the edge of the Kyzylkum.

taxi.fareNote: Most taxis are unmetered, so agree a price first – or use the Yandex Go and inDrive apps, which show fixed fares and are cheaper than flagging a street taxi.

emergency.note: Dial 101 for fire, 102 for police and 103 for ambulance; 112 also works from mobile phones.

hood_desc: The lively central spine along Al-Khorezmi Avenue, lined with the central bazaar, restaurants, hotels and the Al-Khwarizmi statue; the best base for walking and catching taxis to Khiva.
A broad tree-lined avenue anchored by the Al-Beruni monument and served by Urgench's tram, with Soviet-era civic buildings, shops and cafes; central and easy to get around.
The area around the railway station where overnight trains from Tashkent and Bukhara arrive, with cheap hotels and shared-taxi stands; handy but functional rather than pretty.
A quiet zone by Urgench International Airport barely 4 km from the centre, convenient for early Khiva excursions and short transit stays.
A greener residential district along the Shavat Canal and city park, with local eateries and a calmer, everyday-Khorezm feel away from the traffic.

water.note: Drink bottled water; tap water in the Khorezm region is not potable.

transit.hours: Buses, marshrutkas and the tram run from around 6 AM to 9-10 PM; shared taxis fill the later hours.
transit.note: Urgench is one of the few Uzbek cities with a tram line; that plus city buses, marshrutka minibuses and cheap shared taxis cover the town, and shared taxis are the usual way to reach Khiva 35 km away.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (a few thousand so'm) to the driver or conductor; contactless payment is appearing on some buses.

bus: Shared taxis and marshrutkas to Khiva, Bukhara and the railway station
train: Urgench railway station – overnight and express trains to Tashkent, Samarkand and Bukhara

transit.m: Taxi to the city centre (8-10 min), or straight on to Khiva (~35 km, 45 min)
Marshrutka or city bus toward the centre

tip.r: Tipping is not customary; rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% at tourist restaurants is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Shivit oshi
food.desc: Khorezm's signature dill noodles - startling green hand-cut pasta under a meat, potato and vegetable stew with a spoon of sour cream.

places.name: Terrassa Cafe
places.note: The best-known terrace in old Khiva; rooftop views of Kalta Minor and a set menu built around shivit oshi.

places.name: Khorezm Art Restaurant
places.note: Courtyard restaurant inside the walled city, long recommended for its Khorezm regional cooking.

places.name: Bir Gumbaz
places.note: Right in front of the blue minaret; local dishes plus good desserts and friendly service.

food.name: Tukhum barak
food.desc: Khorezm egg dumplings - thin dough pouches filled with beaten egg and butter, boiled briefly and eaten with sour cream.

places.name: Khorezm Art Restaurant
places.note: One of the few kitchens that reliably makes this fiddly regional speciality to order.

places.name: Terrassa Cafe
places.note: Included on the tasting set menu alongside shivit oshi and steamed dumplings.

places.name: Zerafshan Restaurant
places.note: Traditional dining hall near the walls serving Khorezm home cooking to groups and walk-ins.

food.name: Khorezm plov
food.desc: Uzbekistan's national rice dish, cooked here in a lighter Khorezm style with lamb, carrot, chickpeas and whole garlic in a kazan.

places.name: Urgench Dehqon Bozori
places.note: Market food rows where cooks ladle plov from huge kazans until the pot runs out around lunchtime.

places.name: Zerafshan Restaurant
places.note: Dependable full plates of plov and shashlik a short walk from the Itchan Kala gates.

places.name: Terrassa Cafe
places.note: Tourist-friendly version served with salad and green tea on the rooftop.

food.name: Shashlik
food.desc: Charcoal-grilled skewers of lamb, beef or minced kebab, dusted with cumin and served over raw onion rings and flatbread.

places.name: Urgench Dehqon Bozori
places.note: Grill stalls fire up around the bazaar entrance; the cheapest and smokiest skewers in the region.

places.name: Bir Gumbaz
places.note: Skewers grilled in view of the minaret, a favourite evening stop inside the old city.

places.name: Cafe Zerafshan
places.note: Reliable grill kitchen popular with drivers and guides between Urgench and Khiva.

food.name: Tandir somsa and gumma
food.desc: Clay-oven pastries stuffed with minced lamb, onion and fat - somsa baked on the tandoor wall, gumma fried flat and crisp.

places.name: Urgench Dehqon Bozori
places.note: Tandoor bakers work through the morning; buy them scalding hot straight off the oven wall.

places.name: Street bakeries, Ota Darvoza gate
places.note: Cluster of tandirs by the main entrance to the walled city selling somsa and non bread.

places.name: Terrassa Cafe
places.note: Serves gumma as part of its Khorezm tasting plates if you want it sitting down.

food.name: Manti and lagman
food.desc: Steamed lamb-and-onion dumplings, and hand-pulled noodles in a peppery broth with mutton and vegetables - Silk Road staples.

places.name: Khorezm Art Restaurant
places.note: Handmade manti and noodles in a shaded courtyard inside the mud walls.

places.name: Zerafshan Restaurant
places.note: Big portions of lagman at local prices, popular with Uzbek families.

food.name: Kok choy (green tea)
food.desc: The default drink of Khorezm - a pot of green tea poured into small bowls, refilled endlessly and drunk with every meal.

places.name: Chaikhana at Alloqulikhan Madrasa
places.note: Teahouse tables set in a madrasa courtyard; the classic place to sit out the afternoon heat.

places.name: Terrassa Cafe
places.note: Tea with a rooftop view over the old city at sunset.

places.name: Urgench Dehqon Bozori
places.note: Market teahouses serve pots of green tea with bread for pocket change.

food.name: Ayran and fruit kompot
food.desc: Salted yoghurt drink to cut the desert heat, and jugs of home-made kompot stewed from apricots, cherries or apples.

places.name: Urgench Dehqon Bozori
places.note: Dairy rows sell fresh ayran and katyk by the cup straight from the producers.

places.name: Khorezm Art Restaurant
places.note: House-made kompot served by the jug alongside the Khorezm menu.

places.name: Bir Gumbaz
places.note: Cold kompot and ayran, a welcome break from tea in summer.

landmarks: Urganch's grand monument to the Khorezmshah warrior-hero who resisted Genghis Khan, centred on a proud equestrian statue and landscaped memorial square.
A statue honouring the great ninth-century Khorezmian mathematician whose name gave us 'algorithm', a fitting emblem for this ancient land of scholars.
A soaring memorial celebrating the Avesta, Zoroastrianism's sacred text linked to ancient Khorezm, set in a formal park on the city's edge.
One of the world's quirkiest transit rides, this interurban trolleybus trundles thirty-plus kilometres between Urganch and Khiva's old-city gates.
Museum of Contemporary Art of Uzbekistan
A public museum in Urgench dedicated to contemporary Uzbek painting, sculpture and applied art, cited in the city's official profile as an active cultural institution.
Monument to the Twenty Komsomol Members
A Soviet-era memorial in central Urgench honoring twenty local Komsomol members killed by Tekke basmachi fighters during the 1922 unrest, a recognized historical marker in the city.
The city's rebuilt main train station on the Turkmenabat–Beyneu line, serving as the terminus for the overnight sleeper trains linking Urgench with Tashkent and Samarkand.

train.note: Overnight and high-speed trains link Urgench with Bukhara, Samarkand and Tashkent; the Sharq and express services are the comfortable long-distance option, operated by Uzbekistan Railways.

bus.note: Shared taxis and marshrutkas run constantly to Khiva (35 km, ~45 min) and less often across the Kyzylkum desert to Bukhara.

ferry.note: Urgench stands on the Amu Darya in doubly landlocked Uzbekistan, but the river carries no scheduled passenger traffic and the Aral Sea it once fed has largely dried up, so there are no ferries.

full.name: Ayaz Kala & Toprak Kala
full.blurb: Ancient desert fortresses of old Khorezm (the 'Elliq Qala') rising from the edge of the Kyzylkum.

full.name: Nukus & the Savitsky Museum
full.blurb: Karakalpakstan's capital, home to a world-renowned collection of banned Soviet avant-garde art, about 3 hours northwest.

full.name: Moynaq (Aral Sea ship graveyard)
full.blurb: Rusting ships stranded on the former Aral seabed – a long but striking desert day trip.

half.name: Khiva (Itchan Kala)
half.blurb: The walled UNESCO old city of madrasas, minarets and palaces, 35 km and about 45 minutes away – the reason most travelers come.

half.name: Itchan Kala, Khiva
half.blurb: Thirty minutes away, Khiva's UNESCO-listed walled inner city is a living museum of minarets, madrasas and mud-brick lanes, the region's unmissable highlight.

half.name: Ayaz Kala Fortress
half.blurb: A trio of dramatic mud-brick desert fortresses from the Kushan era, rising from the Kyzylkum sands amid the ancient 'fifty fortresses' of Khorezm.
